scoreNote: Strong (5): grants the powerful influence of unchosen forces while arguing that constraint is not determination and that denying agency is corrosive; addresses the determinist case directly and answers it; tightly reasoned.

sentences.text: None of us chose our genes, our parents, our native country, or the era we were born into, and these unchosen forces shape us profoundly.
The claim presses this point hard, holding that people's behavior is largely determined by forces not of their own making.

There is deep truth in the claim, because we are shaped far more by circumstance than we like to admit, but largely determined goes too far, because within those constraints human beings still exercise real and meaningful choice.

sections.role: Body — Unchosen forces shape us deeply

sentences.text: It is true that unchosen forces shape our behavior more than our pride allows us to see.
Our genes influence our temperament, our upbringing instills our values, and our culture, class, and circumstances set the range of options we ever face.
A child born into poverty and violence and one born into wealth and security will, on average, behave very differently, and neither chose the conditions that shaped them.
Even our apparent choices are nudged by influences we never notice, from advertising to the opinions of those around us, as psychology repeatedly shows.
So the claim is right that much of what we do flows from forces we did not make.
We are, to a striking degree, the products of conditions we never selected.

sections.role: Body — But constraint is not determination

sentences.text: However, that forces shape our behavior does not mean they wholly determine it.
People in nearly identical circumstances behave differently, which would be impossible if circumstance simply dictated conduct.
Two siblings raised in the same home, or two soldiers in the same war, can respond in opposite ways, one with cruelty and the other with courage.
Our unchosen forces set the stage and narrow the options, but within that range we still deliberate, resist, and choose, which is exactly what largely determined denies.
The recovering addict who chooses to quit, the person raised in bigotry who rejects it, and the coward who finds courage all show that circumstance is an influence, not a verdict.
We are shaped by forces beyond our control, but we are not their puppets.
Moreover, to call behavior largely determined is not only inaccurate but corrosive.
If we are merely the products of forces we did not make, then no one is truly responsible for anything, and praise, blame, and effort lose their meaning.
Yet we hold people responsible, and rightly, precisely because we recognize that they could have chosen otherwise within their circumstances.
The belief in our own agency, that we can choose even against the pressures upon us, is also what makes change possible, for individuals and societies alike.
A person convinced he is wholly determined has already surrendered the freedom he in fact possesses.
In conclusion, our behavior is powerfully shaped, but not largely determined, by forces beyond our control.
Circumstance sets the stage and limits our options, yet within those limits we genuinely choose, so the claim is right about the power of forces but wrong to dissolve our responsibility into them.
We are neither free of our circumstances nor enslaved by them, but free within them, and that freedom is the part that matters most.
